Practice (what): Get some natural light outdoors soon after you wake up
Details: Step outside, for example with your morning drink or on your way out. Being outdoors matters more than what you do there, because daylight is far brighter than indoor lighting.
Evidence: Light is one of the main signals your body clock uses to keep time, and research shows that morning light helps set your circadian rhythm. A little natural light soon after waking helps your body know the day has started. A study of over 400,000 UK adults also found that each extra hour spent outdoors in daylight was linked with an earlier body clock, finding it easier to get up and fewer insomnia symptoms.

Details: Choose a gentle style that includes postures, breathing and relaxation, and tell the teacher about any injuries. Move within a comfortable range and stop if you feel pain, dizziness or unwell.

Practice (what): Pause and name what you're feeling in one or two words
Details:
You might do this when you notice a strong feeling, or at a set time like lunch: ask yourself 'What am I feeling right now?' and pick the words that fit best. Use the list below if it helps:
Calm: calm, content, relaxed, peaceful, safe, grateful
Sad: sad, lonely, disappointed, hurt, discouraged, hopeless
Anxious: anxious, worried, nervous, uneasy, overwhelmed, afraid
Angry: angry, frustrated, irritated, annoyed, resentful, furious
Self-conscious: embarrassed, ashamed, guilty, insecure, inadequate, rejected
Energised: excited, curious, interested, motivated, confident, inspired
Evidence: A brain-imaging study found that putting emotions into words reduced activity in the amygdala, the part of the brain that responds to emotional threats. Naming what you feel, even in a word or two, may help take the edge off difficult emotions.

Practice (what): Write down one problem that's on your mind and list at least three possible ways to tackle it
Frequency and time: for about 10 minutes, once a week
Details: Describe the problem in one or two specific sentences, then list options without judging them yet. Treat it as a challenge you can work on, not a sign that something is wrong with you.
Evidence: The research found that structured problem-solving programmes reduced distress, and worked better when they included a hopeful attitude towards problems as well as practical skills. Defining the problem clearly and listing options are the first two steps.

Practice (what): Write about an emotionally important experience
Frequency and time: for 15 minutes, on 3 days close together
Details: Find somewhere private and write freely about the experience and your deepest thoughts and feelings about it. Don't worry about spelling or grammar. It's normal to feel a little stirred up afterwards. If it feels overwhelming, stop and choose a less intense topic, or talk to someone you trust. If you've recently been through a traumatic event or bereavement, or are being treated for PTSD, check with your doctor or therapist before doing this.
Evidence: Reviews of randomised trials show that writing about your deepest thoughts and feelings brings a small but lasting easing of stress and low mood, often noticed weeks later rather than straight away. Sessions held a day or two apart work best.

Evidence: The research found that savouring practices led to moderate improvements in positive emotions and wellbeing and reduced negative emotional symptoms across 20 randomised trials. In one experiment, savouring the moment after a stressful hassle boosted positive emotions more than other approaches.

Respiratory and cardiovascular responses to walking down a traffic-polluted road compared with walking in a traffic-free area in participants aged 60 years and older with chronic lung or heart disease and age-matched healthy controls: a randomised, crossover study. The Lancet, 391(10118), 339–349. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(17)32643-0
Evidence level note: Single primary study in adults over 60; promising but limited evidence.
Why this matters: Walking in green, quieter places may let you get more from your exercise than busy roads allow.
Relevant profiles: City dwellers; Walkers, runners and cyclists; Over 60

When you walk, run or cycle, choose parks or quieter streets over busy roads when you can.
Plan your usual routes through parks, back streets or riverside paths, even if it adds a few minutes.

Practice (what): Limit burning wood, candles or incense indoors, and use an extractor fan or open a window
Details: Ventilate especially when cooking on a gas hob, and avoid burning candles or incense in closed rooms.
Evidence: A review of 116 studies found that cooking and heating with polluting fuels such as wood or charcoal was linked with more lung disease, and gas cooking with slightly more than electric. Ventilating while cooking and limiting indoor burning can help cut down the smoke and fine particles you breathe.
References: Puzzolo, E., Fleeman, N., Lorenzetti, F., Rubinstein, F., Li, Y., Xing, R., Shen, G., Nix, E., Maden, M., Bresnahan, R., Duarte, R., Abebe, L., Lewis, J., Williams, K. N., Adahir-Rohani, H., & Pope, D. (2024). Estimated health effects from domestic use of gaseous fuels for cooking and heating in high-income, middle-income, and low-income countries: a systematic review and meta-analyses. The Lancet Respiratory Medicine, 12(4), 281–293. https://doi.org/10.1016/S2213-2600(23)00427-7
Evidence level note: Observational evidence only, reasonable fit; useful for those cooking or burning indoors.
Why this matters: Ventilating while cooking and limiting indoor burning cuts the smoke and fine particles you breathe.
Relevant profiles: Cooks on gas; Uses wood burners, candles or incense

Practice (what): Learn a small new skill
Details: Try a few words in a new language, a new recipe, a song, a chord or a card trick.
Evidence: A review of 22 studies with more than 29,000 people found that those with more education, more complex jobs or more mentally stimulating pastimes were much less likely to develop dementia, and the more mentally stimulating activity people did in later life, the lower their risk. Learning something new is a simple first step.
References: Valenzuela, M. J., & Sachdev, P. (2006). Brain reserve and dementia: a systematic review. Psychological Medicine, 36(4), 441–454. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0033291705006264
Evidence level note: Observational evidence only, reasonable fit; light, optional first step.
Why this matters: Learning something new keeps your mind active and is an easy, enjoyable habit to start.
Relevant profiles: Most adults; Over 60
Previous practice text (before the split:
Learn something new this week, such as a few words in a new language, a new recipe or a song.
Pick something small you can learn in a few minutes, such as a phrase, a chord, a card trick or a new recipe.

Practice (what): Practise a new skill that stretches you
Details: Choose something new to you, such as an instrument, a language or a craft, and practise it at the same time each week.
Evidence: Studies link regular, complex mental activity with a lower risk of dementia, and a trial found that older adults who spent three months learning demanding new skills, such as digital photography, improved their memory more than those doing social or easy activities.
References: Valenzuela, M. J., & Sachdev, P. (2006). Brain reserve and dementia: a systematic review. Psychological Medicine, 36(4), 441–454. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0033291705006264 | Park, D. C., Lodi-Smith, J., Drew, L., Haber, S., Hebrank, A., Bischof, G. N., & Aamodt, W. (2014). The impact of sustained engagement on cognitive function in older adults: the Synapse Project. Psychological Science, 25(1), 103–112. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797613499592
Evidence level note: Mixed trial and observational evidence; most relevant to brain health in later life.
Why this matters: Regularly stretching your mind with a new skill may help keep your memory sharp.
Relevant profiles: Over 60; Retired or reduced work; Beginners to new hobbies

Practice (what): Practise a demanding new skill
Frequency and time: for 1 hour, 4 days a week, building up gradually
Details: Choose a skill you'd enjoy getting good at, such as photography, a language or an instrument, and take a course or join a class. Build up your practice time over several months.
Evidence: In a randomised trial, older adults who spent about 16 hours a week for three months learning quilting or digital photography improved their memory more than those doing social or less demanding activities.
References: Park, D. C., Lodi-Smith, J., Drew, L., Haber, S., Hebrank, A., Bischof, G. N., & Aamodt, W. (2014). The impact of sustained engagement on cognitive function in older adults: the Synapse Project. Psychological Science, 25(1), 103–112. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797613499592
Evidence level note: Single primary trial in older adults; promising but a big time commitment.
Why this matters: Getting properly good at a demanding new skill may help boost your memory.
Relevant profiles: Over 60; Retired or reduced work; Has free time
Caution / referral trigger: Build up gradually to avoid burnout
Comes next: Top level: keep it as a habit, or choose another practice in the same theme
